note: W1-LIBRARY round 3. The Argonian half of the martial library, written so the province's own arms are not described only by the people occupying it — RI-LOR03 'how we lose' #6. Six of the seven are Argonian-authored. Between them they cover axes-maces, claw-fang, polearms, marksman, shieldcraft and greatweapons, all of which scored zero across the previous 70 books. Three declared contradictions, none of them adjudicated anywhere: whether a shield that cannot parry is worth carrying, whether the high grip on the ricasso is worth its reach, and whether the reaping blades were weapons before they were duties.

books.title: The Splitting of Shells, and What Else the Same Stroke Does
books.author: Ojal-Aneesh, shell-cutter at Hollow-Reeds, who was asked for a tool book and has given what he has
books.unreliability: He begins as a craftsman and ends as something else, and the turn happens in the middle of a paragraph about a hinge. He knows it has happened. He apologises for it once and then keeps going. His account of the raid he was in is the least reliable thing in the book and the only part anyone quotes.
books.text:
This one was asked by the Provincial Office for a book on the cutting of shells, for the use of factors who buy them, and this one has written it, and the Office will find that it is not the book it asked for. This one is sorry. The tool does what the tool does and a book about the tool goes where the tool goes.

ON THE AXE ITSELF.

The shell-splitter is a wood-axe with the beard drawn out longer and the poll left heavy. Nothing about it was invented. It is what a boat-builder's axe becomes when it is used on shell for two generations and the smith is told, each time, to make the next one a little more like the last one that worked.

The head is heavy because shell is hard and does not care about an edge. A sharp light axe skids off a great-shell's back and takes the man's shin. A heavy dull one goes in. Keep it heavy. Keep it only as sharp as it needs to be to bite and no sharper, and never let a Cyrodiil armourer put an edge on it for you, because they cannot help themselves and they will take the weight out of it while they are doing it.

The haft is as long as your arm from the pit to the fingers. Longer and you cannot work close in a boat. Shorter and you are hitting with your wrist, and your wrist will be finished before you are 30.

THE FOUR CUTS OF THE SHELL.

1. The seam. Every shell has one and it runs where the two halves were joined when the thing was young. Find it with the thumb before you find it with the axe. A shell opened along its seam takes 3 strokes. A shell opened anywhere else takes 20 and ruins the meat.

2. The hinge. This is the work. The hinge is a plug of gristle at the back, thick as your forearm and tougher than rope, and it is why the shell will not open even after the seam is cut. You cannot chop a hinge. You have tried, everyone has tried, the young ones try it every season. It gives with the blow and closes again.

The hinge is taken with a stroke that goes in and then travels sideways, downward and toward you, so that the beard of the axe is drawn through the gristle rather than driven into it. Not a chop. A chop and a pull, in one motion, and the pull is the part that does the work.

Learn it on a bad shell that you do not mind spoiling. It takes most people a season. It took this one two, and this one's mother said things.

3. The clean. Small strokes, the axe held up near the head with the hand over the beard, the way you would hold a knife. Anyone can do this after a morning.

4. The lift. Not a cut. The poll under the lip and lever.

NOW THE THING THIS ONE DID NOT MEAN TO WRITE.

The hinge stroke is the stroke that takes a shield.

This one found this out at Hollow-Reeds in the season of the second raid, and this one is going to set it down badly because it was a bad afternoon and this one's memory of it is not a good witness.

There were men off a boat. They had come up the channel and they had come for the drying-racks and they had shields, small round ones, hide over reed. This one had an axe because this one was cutting when they came, and this one did what this one does 40 times in a working day.

The axe went over the top edge of the man's shield. The beard came down behind it. And then this one pulled, sideways and down and toward, exactly as one takes a hinge, because that is the only stroke this one's arm has ever learned to finish.

The shield came off his arm. It did not break. The straps did not break. His arm came down with it and then his shoulder came down with it and then he was leaning forward with his face where his shield had been, and he was surprised, and this one was more surprised than he was.

This one wants to be careful here. This one did not do anything clever. This one did the only stroke this one knows and the shield happened to be a hinge.

WHAT THIS ONE HAS SINCE BEEN TOLD.

An Imperial serjeant came through in the dry season and this one asked him about it, because it had been sitting badly.

He said: yes. He said the Legion has a name for it and drills it and puts it in a book, and the book calls it taking the rim, and every axeman in the cohorts is taught to go for the edge of a shield and not the middle of it. He said the middle of a shield is where a shield is a shield and the edge is where it is a piece of wood with a strap on the back.

He said something else that this one has thought about since. He said: the reason we teach it and you already knew it is that we had to work it out, and you had to open shellfish.

This one asked him whether that was a compliment. He laughed and did not answer, and then he bought two axes for the cohort at 40 drakes each, which was robbery, and this one let him.

WHAT THIS ONE WILL AND WILL NOT SAY.

The Provincial Office asked for a book about a tool and will get this. The Office may strike what it likes.

This one will not write down how to fight with an axe, because this one does not know how to fight with an axe, and the difference between knowing how to open a hinge and knowing how to fight is a difference measured in the number of people who are dead who should not be.

What this one will say is this. A shell-cutter at Hollow-Reeds has already done the hard part of it, 40 times a day, for years, and does not know it, and will find out on the worst afternoon of their life if nobody tells them first.

So: it is the same stroke. In and sideways and down and toward you. On the rim and not the face.

There. Now the Office has its book.

The best hafts are grown, not cut. Ask at Hollow-Reeds for a stick that has been trained crooked in the second year, and pay what is asked, and do not haggle with a woman who has spent 8 years bending a tree for you.

ON THE HAFT, PROPERLY, BECAUSE THE OFFICE WILL WANT IT.

A grown haft is a stick that has been trained crooked while it was alive, so that the grain runs round the bend instead of across it.

A cut haft has the grain going one way and the bend put in afterwards by a man with steam, and the grain does not care about the steam, and the first hard stroke into a hinge finds the place where the grain crosses the bend and the haft goes there, and it goes without any warning at all, and the head comes off toward whatever is in front of you.

This one has had 2 cut hafts break and has never had a grown one break. This one is not saying it cannot happen. This one is saying it has not happened here in this one's lifetime.

Training a haft is 8 years of somebody going out to a particular sapling in a particular month and moving a cord. It is done by the old and it is done for grandchildren, and the reason the price is what it is has nothing to do with the wood.

REPAIR, AND WHAT NOT TO DO.

The head loosens. It always loosens. This is not a fault, it is what happens when you drive iron into wood in a wet country, and a shell-cutter checks the head every morning the way a poler checks a pole.

Wedge it from the top with a shell wedge and never with an iron one. An iron wedge splits the haft along its length in about a season and the split is inside the eye where you cannot see it.

Do not soak the head to swell the wood. Everyone does this. It works for a week and it rusts the eye from the inside and the head will come off in the second season instead of the fifth.

If the beard chips, do not grind the chip out. Grinding a beard back changes the curve, and the curve is the whole of the hinge stroke, and this one has watched a good cutter lose a season's skill because a smith at Gideon tidied their axe for them.

MORE ABOUT THE AFTERNOON, BECAUSE THIS ONE HAS BEEN ASKED.

Three people have come to Hollow-Reeds to ask about it and this one has told all 3 the same and will set it down once.

There were 6 men off the boat. This one has been told since that there were 4 and has been told since that there were 9. This one counted 6 at the time and this one was not counting.

The one whose shield came off was not killed by this one. He went down and he got up and he went back to the boat holding his arm and this one has thought about him for years, and this one hopes he is alive, and this one is aware that hoping is a cheap thing to do about somebody you took a shield off.

Two people from this settlement were killed. Sesh-Anaat's brother, who was 19, and a woman whose name this one will not write because her family has asked.

The racks were not taken.

WHAT A SHELL-CUTTER SHOULD DO IF IT HAPPENS TO THEM.

This one said above that this one will not write down how to fight with an axe and this one meant it. But a thing has been sitting badly since and this one is going to put it in.

Do not chase. This is the whole of the advice.

An axe is a stroke you make when a thing has come to you. It is not a stroke you carry across a yard. The moment you take a step toward somebody with an axe up, you have given them the space to come inside it, and inside it you are an unarmed person holding a heavy stick by the wrong end.

Stand where you were standing. Let them come. Do the one thing you have done 40 times a day since you were 9.

Then stop, and look at what you have done, and be sick if you need to be, and do not let anybody at Gideon buy you a drink about it afterwards.

books.title: What the Hand Knows: A Teaching for Those Who Will Not Carry
books.author: set down at Helstrom by Weeth-Ei-Vakh, who teaches the young that are given to her and does not say by whom
books.unreliability: A teaching text that will not name its school, and the refusal is the most informative thing in it. Two of the four lessons are about not being armed at all, which is either a spiritual position or a practical one about being searched, and she does not say which, and there is reason to think she means both.
books.text:
This is for the ones who come to me with nothing in their hands. Because they have been told to come with nothing in their hands. Or because they have nothing.

I will not say who tells them. I will not say what the teaching is for. If you have been sent to me you already know. If you have not been sent to me, this is a book about how the hand works, and you may read it as one.

THE FIRST LESSON. WHERE YOU LIVE.

A sword lives at a sword's length. A spear lives at a spear's length. A claw lives at no length at all.

Everyone who fights carries a ring around themselves. The ring is as wide as their weapon. Inside it they are strong. Outside it they are nothing. A man with a long weapon has a wide ring and has spent his life learning to keep you at the edge of it.

The hand has no ring. The hand has a place. The place is against him. Chest to chest. Close enough to feel him decide.

So the whole of what I teach is the crossing. Everything before the crossing. Nothing after it. After the crossing the fight is over one way or the other, and no teaching reaches there.

THE SECOND LESSON. THE CLAW IS NOT A KNIFE.

The young ones want the claw to be a small knife. It is not. A claw used as a small knife will be beaten by a small knife every time. A knife is longer. It is straighter. It was made by somebody whose whole trade was making it.

A claw is a hook that is part of you.

Understand that and you have the school. A knife may be dropped. Taken. Parried away. Put on a table at a door. A claw cannot be separated from the hand. So the claw can hold.

You may take a wrist and keep it. You may take a collar and keep it. You may take the edge of a shield with four fingers of the left hand and keep it. And while you are keeping it you have both of your feet and one of his.

The fang is for after the hold. Never before. A young one who leads with the teeth has told the other person what they are. That gives away the only advantage of arriving with nothing in the hands. Nobody watches an empty hand.

THE THIRD LESSON. THE ROOM.

Where does the hand win.

Doorways. Stairs. The inside of a boat. A corridor at Xanmeer with a low roof. Anywhere a long weapon cannot finish the motion it needs to finish. A halberd in a hallway is a stick.

Where does the hand lose. Open ground. Standing water above the knee. Three of them. And anybody who has understood the first lesson and simply walks backwards.

A man walking backwards with a spear beats every hand in this province. I have never taught a young one who believed me until it was done to them.

So you do not fight in open ground. You wait. You go where the ground is on your side. Or you do not go.

THE FOURTH LESSON. WHICH IS THE ONE THEY DO NOT LIKE.

You will be searched.

At the gate at Gideon. At the customs house. At the head of every jetty in the province where a man with a list is paid to look at people.

They will find a knife. They will find a hook sewn into a sleeve. They will find the clever thing you made and were proud of.

They will not find the hand.

This is the whole reason the teaching exists. I am tired of pretending otherwise for the benefit of the Office. It is not a purity. It is not a discipline of the spirit.

My grandmother's grandmother was taught it. She was taught it because the people who taught her were not permitted to carry anything. The people who did the permitting are still here. They still have lists.

I say this plainly to the young ones on the first day. Some of them go home. Good.

THE LAST THING.

They will tell you the claw is a poor weapon. It is a poor weapon. Any tooth-and-nail creature in this marsh has better claws than you and dies to a farmer with a stick.

The hand is not a good weapon. The hand is the weapon that is still there after they have taken the others.

And a poor weapon that is present has beaten a fine weapon that is at the gate more often than the histories admit. The histories were written by people who were allowed to carry things.

When you have learned this, learn a spear. I mean it. Learn a spear. Carry it openly. Use it. Be the one with the long ring.

And on the day somebody takes it off you at a jetty and smiles about it, you will walk in with your hands open like everybody else.

books.title: The Gig and the Lance: Two Uncles Disagreeing, Set Down by a Nephew Who Is Sick of It
books.author: Jaseeth-of-the-Weirs, nephew to both of them, at Lilmoth
books.unreliability: The nephew claims to be impartial and is plainly on his uncle Sul's side, which he gives away by writing Sul's arguments in full sentences and Deej's in fragments. He also puts a conclusion in the last paragraph that neither uncle would sign.
books.text:
My uncle Sul holds a spear underhand. My uncle Deej holds a spear overhand. They have not eaten at the same table since the flood year and my mother has asked me to write down what each of them says so that the family may stop hearing it.

I have written both. I have tried to be fair. My mother will say I have not been.

WHAT A GIG IS.

Both of them agree this far, so I will put it first.

A fisher's gig is a spear with barbs, on a shaft as long as a man and half a man, and it is for taking fish out of water that is moving. Every household on the weirs has 3 or 4. Every child learns it. It is not a weapon and everyone in this province has one, and those two facts together are the whole reason anybody argues about it.

UNCLE SUL, WHO HOLDS IT UNDERHAND.

Sul is a weir-man and has been since he was 9. He holds the gig at the hip, the butt of the shaft trapped against the body under the elbow, the point low and forward, and he moves the point by moving his feet.

He says: the water is the enemy and not the fish.

He says: a fish in moving water is not where you see it, and the only thing you can trust is your own body, and if the spear is *part* of your body — trapped against your side, driven by your legs — then you will put it where you meant to. If it is out at the end of your arms it is a separate creature and the two of you must agree, and you will not agree in time.

He says: braced at the hip, you may drive with your whole weight and the water cannot push the point aside, because to push it aside it must push all of you aside.

He says: and if the thing at the other end is heavy and comes at you, the butt is already against your body and the ground is already behind your foot, and you have made a wall out of a stick.

He says the marsh-lance men look very fine and drown.

UNCLE DEEJ, WHO HOLDS IT OVERHAND.

Deej was a levy for 6 years at Stormhold and came back with opinions.

He holds it above the shoulder, palm up under the shaft, point angled downward, and he throws the point down into the thing rather than pushing it forward.

He says: reach. Says the underhand hold gives away a forearm and a shoulder of length and that a forearm is a life.

He says: down. Says everything worth hitting in this country is below you — a man in a boat, a man in water, a thing coming up out of it — and a point that is already angled downward does not have to be turned.

He says: over the shield. That's his best one and he knows it. A low point goes into a shield. A high point that comes down goes over the top of one and into a collarbone, and a shield that is lifted to stop it is a shield that is not covering the belly, and one of Sul's people is standing there with a gig at the hip.

He says: and you can throw it. Says Sul cannot throw his and Sul says he does not want to throw his because then he hasn't got it.

He says the weir-men fight standing still like posts and get walked around.

WHAT I HAVE SEEN.

I have fished with both of them and I will say the true thing, which is that Sul takes more fish and Deej takes bigger ones.

Sul's hold does not miss. In fast water off the weir at Hollow-Reeds I have watched him take 30 in an afternoon with the point never going more than a hand's width from where he intended. But everything he takes is within a body's length of him.

Deej's hold misses often and reaches into water Sul cannot touch at all. When a great eel came up in the channel below Lilmoth two seasons ago, Sul stood and watched and Deej put a lance into it from a boat length away, and afterwards Sul said Deej had been lucky, and Deej said that he had been lucky 4 times that season and Sul had been unlucky none.

WHAT THE ARMY SAYS, FOR WHAT IT IS WORTH.

The garrison at Lilmoth teaches the underhand hold to its spearmen and the overhand to nobody, and when I asked a serjeant why he said: because a man in a rank who lifts his spear above his shoulder puts it through the head of the man behind him.

Which is an answer about ranks and not an answer about spears. I told Deej this and he was pleased for a week.

WHAT I THINK, AND MY MOTHER WILL BE ANGRY.

They are both describing where they stand.

Sul stands on a weir. A weir does not move. He has built his whole method on the certainty that his feet are on something, and on a weir he is unbeatable and I would not fight him for anything.

Deej stands in a boat. A boat moves. He gave up the braced hold because he has never in his life had anything to brace against, and so he learned to put the point somewhere from the arms alone, which is harder and less certain and works when you are floating.

So the question is not which hold is better. The question is what is under your feet, and everybody in this family has been shouting about spears for 9 years when they should have been talking about ground.

I am going to give this to my mother now and go and stay with my aunt.

books.title: The Horn and the Wet String: On Bows in a Country That Ruins Them
books.author: Ixina-Sheel, bowyer, third generation, at Archon, and she has signed it because the last one was attributed to her father
books.unreliability: A first-rate technical writer with one blind spot she has inherited from her father: she treats the chitin recurve as a degraded imitation of the horn bow rather than a different answer to a different problem, and every measurement she reports supports the reading she refuses to make.
books.wrong_on_purpose: Calls the chitin recurve a cheap imitation of the horn-and-sinew bow. Her own figures show it losing almost nothing in the wet while the horn bow loses everything, which is the opposite of a degradation.
books.text:
My father sold horn bows in this province for forty-one years, and he told every customer who came into the shop the same thing, and the thing he told them was perfectly true in the dry season.

I am going to write down what is true in the other season, because he would not, and because I have been repairing his bows since I was twelve years old and I know what comes back through the door.

WHAT A HORN BOW IS.

A belly of horn, a back of sinew, a core of wood between the two of them, and glue holding the whole arrangement together. It is the finest bow that anybody has ever made, storing more in a short limb than any self bow of twice the length, and it will outshoot anything on this continent.

The glue is fish glue and hide glue, and it is soluble in water, and every word of the rest of this book follows from that one sentence.

WHAT HAPPENS TO ONE HERE.

In the wet season, unsealed, the bow delaminates, and it does not do it slowly. I have had one come back to the shop where the sinew backing had lifted along a hand's length in nine days of standing in a hut with a leaking roof, and nobody had shot it wrong, and nobody had done anything to it at all; it sat in the air of this province and it came apart.

In the wet season, sealed with lacquer and kept in a case, the bow survives and loses draw weight regardless, because the horn takes up water through the ends where you have cut it and the limbs go lazy. I have measured this across a wet season on my father's own bow, and it drew sixty-two pounds at the beginning and fifty-one at the end, on the same string, with the same arm, and the arrows went where you would expect fifty-one pounds to put them.

The string is worse, and nobody ever talks about the string. A sinew string in this air stretches until the brace height has fallen by two fingers, and a bow at low brace slaps your wrist and throws slow. Waxed linen is better and rots. There is no third option and I have been looking for one for years.

WHAT PEOPLE DO ABOUT IT.

Three things, and I will give each of them its due.

First, they keep the good bow for the dry season and shoot a plain wooden self bow for the rest of the year, which works, and which is what I would advise, and which nobody takes advice about, because a self bow of the length you need in order to get any weight out of it is a stave as tall as you are, and you cannot use such a thing in a boat or in reeds or anywhere else in this country where the reeds are.

Second, they buy the reed shortbow, which is not so much a bow as a way of getting an arrow to travel thirty paces, which every hunting family owns, and of which I sell four for every horn bow that leaves this shop. I will not sneer at it. It is cheap, it does not care about water, a child can draw it, and if you are shooting a bird off a rack at twenty paces then it is the correct tool and my finest work would be an affectation.

Third, and here I must be careful, my father being only three years dead and people at Archon remembering him, they buy the chitin recurve.

ON THE CHITIN RECURVE.

I will describe it fairly and then I will say what I think of it.

The limbs are cut from the shell plate of a great beetle, steamed and set into a recurve and pinned to a short riser rather than glued along their whole length, the belly being the natural inner face of the plate, and there is no sinew backing, no horn, and hardly any glue anywhere that matters.

It is short, the limbs are stubby, and the string angle at full draw is sharp enough to pinch the fingers, so that it is drawn to the chest and not to the cheek, and a man accustomed to a horn bow will shoot low with one for a month.

It does not delaminate, and I have had exactly two of them back in six years, both of which had been trodden on.

It does not lose weight across a season. I measured a well-made one at Archon at forty-seven pounds in Sun's Height and forty-six in Frostfall, and I measured it a second time because I did not believe the first figure.

It throws an arrow a little slower than a horn bow of the same weight, the tips being heavier and the whole thing cruder, and at forty paces it is perhaps a hand's width less certain in the hands of somebody who can shoot.

And it costs a third of what I charge.

Here is what I think of it, and my father thought it before me: it is an imitation, and it is what people buy who cannot afford real work, and every good thing about it is a thing it achieves by not attempting anything difficult. There is no craft in pinning two pieces of shell to a stick, and my apprentice could do it in his second year, and I would not let him sign it.

The province is full of them now, the auxiliaries at Archon carry them and the Cohort buys them by the crate, and I have watched an officer who has shot at Chorrol pick one up and pull a face and put it down again.

I shall keep making horn bows, and my daughter will keep making horn bows, and when the wet season comes and the chitin men are still shooting and my own customers are standing in my shop with a lifted backing and an apologetic expression, I shall repair them, at fifteen drakes, as I have done every year of my life.

A NOTE ON ARROWS, WHICH MATTERS MORE THAN ANY OF THE ABOVE.

Fletching. Feather goes soft and lies down in this air, and an arrow with a lain-down fletch will fishtail out of a good bow and land wherever it likes.

Use split reed, cut thin, set in three, glued with pitch and never with hide. It is heavier than feather, it is noisier in flight, it costs you a little distance, and it does not care about water at all.

The best archer in this province is not the one with the best bow but the one whose arrows are all the same as each other; and I have never met an Imperial officer who believed that when I said it, and I have never met a marsh hunter who needed telling.

books.title: The Door That Walks: On the Great Shields of the Stone Nests, and Why They Cannot Turn a Blow Aside
books.author: Beem-Ei, who keeps the armoury at Helstrom and has carried one for 19 seasons
books.unreliability: Right about the shield and wrong about its history. She has the Xanmeer door coming down from the builders of the stone nests because that is what it is called; the pattern is much younger than she thinks and the name was borrowed. She never considers it, and nothing in the province will tell her otherwise.

contradicts.on: whether a shield that cannot parry is worth carrying

books.text:
There is a thing the Imperial officers say when they first see one of us carrying a door, and they all say it, and after 19 seasons I have stopped finding it funny.

They say: can it parry?

No. It cannot parry. It will never parry. A young one who tries to parry with a Xanmeer door will have their wrist taken off at the joint by their own shield, and I have seen it, and the young one lived and does not carry anything now.

I am going to explain why the answer is no, and why the question is the wrong question, and I am going to have to explain what a parry is first, because the officers who ask do not always know.

WHAT A PARRY IS.

A parry is a small shield moving *toward* a blow at the moment the blow arrives, turning it off its line so that it goes past you, and leaving the man who threw it with his weight in a place he did not want it.

It is a beautiful thing to watch and I cannot do it and I have never wanted to.

Note the two words: small, and moving. A parry is made of timing and of a light thing that may be flicked. The buckler people at Lilmoth do it with a plate the size of a supper dish and they do it in the space of a breath and if they are wrong by that same breath they are opened from the collar down.

Now consider a door. A door is as tall as your chest and as wide as your shoulders and half again, faced with hide over a frame of grown root, and it weighs what a small person weighs. Nothing about it moves quickly. By the time a door has begun to travel toward a blow the blow has been and gone and the door is still travelling, and now it is out of position, and now you are standing behind an open gate holding the gate.

So: no. It cannot parry. It is not a limitation the smith failed to overcome. A door that could be flicked would not be a door.

WHAT IT DOES INSTEAD.

It covers an angle, and the angle is the whole argument.

Every shield covers a wedge, with the point of the wedge at your shoulder and the wide end out in front of you, and anything that arrives inside the wedge meets the shield and anything that arrives outside it meets you. This is not an opinion. Stand a young one in a yard and have people tap them from around a circle and they will learn where their wedge ends inside a morning, and they will remember it for life.

A buckler's wedge is narrow. A small reed target's is a little wider. The Imperial kite covers a good deal and is the best of the middling shields and I will not hear otherwise.

A door covers so wide a wedge that a man on either side of you is inside it.

That is the sentence. Everything the great shields have ever been for is in that sentence. A door is not a defence for the person carrying it. A door is a piece of wall that has agreed to walk, and its purpose is to cover the people who cannot cover themselves — the spear behind you, the bow behind the spear, the one carrying water, the young.

I have stood in a channel at Helstrom with 3 doors abreast and 40 people behind us and we did not strike anybody at all for the length of an afternoon, and not one of the 40 was touched, and I count that the finest day's work of my life.

WHAT IT COSTS.

I will be honest about the cost, because the young ones are told the glory and not the rest.

It is heavy in a way that is difficult to describe to somebody who has not done it. Not heavy like a load; heavy like weather. You are tired before the fight starts. You will be tired after every fight you are ever in, whether you did anything or not.

You cannot go where you like. Reeds, low branches, the inside of a boat, any doorway made for people rather than for doors. There are whole districts of Lilmoth I have never walked down carrying mine.

And you cannot turn quickly. This is the one that kills. Everything is fine while they come at your front, and the moment two of them work out that the answer is to go round, you are a slow person carrying a wall, and the wall is pointing at nobody.

So a door never walks alone. Never. If you are carrying one and you find that the people who were beside you are not beside you any more, put it down and draw whatever else you have, and let somebody else be angry with you afterwards.

TO THE BUCKLER PEOPLE AT LILMOTH, WHO HAVE BEEN RUDE ABOUT US IN PRINT.

You say a shield that cannot parry is half a shield. You say we have taken the cleverness out and left only the weight.

I say: your cleverness protects exactly one person, and it protects them only for as long as their timing holds, and timing is a young person's property and you all know it.

I have carried this for 19 seasons. I am not quick. I was never quick. There is a place in the line for somebody who is not quick and never was, and the buckler schools have no place at all for that person, and the province is full of them, and somebody has to stand in front of the young.

ON WHERE IT COMES FROM.

The pattern is called a Xanmeer door because it is the door of a stone nest, and it is the shape of the doors in the terraces — squared at the top, tapering a little to the foot, the boss set high and off centre where a door's ring would be.

Our grandmothers stacked the world into steps and hung doors in it, and when they had to fight they took the doors off. That is what I was taught at 11 and it is what I teach.

An Imperial antiquarian at Gideon told me the pattern was 300 years old at most and had been named after the ruins by traders who wanted to sell it. I asked him how he knew and he said the joinery. I told him he had never carried one and he agreed, cheerfully, and bought me a drink, and I have thought about it since and I do not intend to think about it again.

THREE ABREAST, WHICH IS THE ONLY FORMATION THERE IS.

A door alone is a slow person carrying a wall. Two doors are 2 slow people carrying 2 walls with a gap between them, and the gap is where you will be killed.

Three is a formation. Three abreast, the middle one half a pace forward, the outer two angled in so that the wedges overlap at the edges and there is no line into the middle that does not cross somebody's shield.

The middle one leads and the outer two watch the outside and nobody watches the front, because the front is covered by the shape and not by anybody's attention.

Behind the 3, at most 4 more people, and they are the reason the formation exists. Spears reaching between us. A bow, if there is one and if there is anywhere for it to shoot. And whoever is being got out.

We move at the pace of the slowest of us and we do not open the shape to go round anything, we go through or we go back, and going back is done by walking backwards and not by turning, and walking backwards in mud carrying a door is the single hardest thing I have ever learned to do and I still cannot do it well at 44.

THE WET SEASON.

Everything above is for hard ground and there is not much hard ground.

In standing water the door is worse than useless below the waterline, because the bottom edge catches the water when you move and the water is heavier than the shield. You must lift it, and lifting it uncovers your legs, and there are things in the water.

So in the wet season we carry them higher and shorter and we accept the legs. A door-carrier in a wet season is armoured from the chin to the hip and naked below and knows it, and this is why we do not stand in water if the ground behind us is dry, and why 3 doors at the mouth of a channel is a fine thing and 3 doors in the middle of one is a mistake nobody survives to make twice.

WHO SHOULD NOT CARRY ONE.

The quick. Truly. A quick person carrying a door will try to use it quickly and will be out of position, and the whole point of the shape is that nothing in it moves except at the pace of the shape. I have refused doors to 4 young ones and all 4 were the best of their year and all 4 were furious.

Anybody with a bad back, and I mean anybody who has ever mentioned their back once.

Anybody who has something to prove. This weapon is carried in front of people who cannot cover themselves and it is not a place to find out things about yourself.

And anybody who cannot bear to be shouted at while doing nothing, because that is most of the work. You will stand and hold, and behind you people will be doing the things that are remembered afterwards, and nobody will describe your afternoon at all.

WHAT WE ARE CALLED, AND WHAT I THINK ABOUT IT.

The buckler people at Lilmoth call us the door-carriers and they do not mean it kindly.

I have carried this for 19 seasons and I will be carrying it until my back goes and then I will be teaching it, and I would like whoever comes after me to know that the name is correct. That is what we are. Somebody carries the door.

I would only say to Vaneia Corr, who I am told is a fine teacher and who I would like to meet: you sell a breath. I have read your book and it is a good book and the breath is real and I cannot take it.

I sell an afternoon in which nobody behind me was touched. It is a duller thing to sell. There are 40 people at Helstrom who bought it.

books.title: Why the Fen Lads Beat the Chorrol Man, Written Out Because He Keeps Asking
books.author: Halgrid Two-Winters, auxiliary, Ninth Cohort, Blackrose levy, and his mother was from Dunstad
books.unreliability: He explains the mechanical advantage correctly and by accident, in the course of describing a bout, and then draws the wrong lesson from it in his own last paragraph. He also believes Cray has refused him out of contempt. Cray has refused him out of fear of being humiliated in front of paying pupils, which everyone in the yard except Halgrid can see.

contradicts.on: whether the high grip on the ricasso is worth the reach it gives up

books.text:
Master Cray has printed a book saying the way I hold my sword is a fashion and that when I'm 40 my wrists will have gone and I'll come to him and he won't say anything.

I've asked him 3 times for a bout. He says a demonstration proves what the two men in it can do and not what the method can do. Which is fine, only he printed a book about the method, so.

I'm not a writer. Cohort clerk's doing the spelling. This is what I actually do and why, and anyone who wants can decide.

WHAT THE HOLD IS.

A greatsword's got a long blunt bit above the crossguard before the edge starts. Ricasso, the Nords call it, my mother called it the dull span. You put your leading hand there, on the flat, over the guard. Right hand stays on the grip.

So instead of two hands close together on a handle with 5 feet of sword out in front, you've got two hands a forearm apart with 4 feet of sword out in front and a forearm of it behind your left hand.

Cray's right that you lose reach. You lose about a forearm. He's right about the hand being outside the guard too, and I've got a scar across two knuckles that agrees with him, and I'd still not go back.

WHY IT ACTUALLY WINS AND I DON'T THINK CRAY KNOWS.

He says it looks faster because a shorter lever always looks faster, and that a stroke arriving from closer in hasn't gone faster, it's gone less far. And he says you could get the same by standing nearer.

That's the bit that's wrong and it's wrong in an interesting way.

It's not about how fast the sword gets there. It's about how fast it comes BACK and goes the other way.

Look. With hands together on the handle, the whole sword is out in front of you, and all its weight is at the far end of a long stick you're holding at one end. When you've swung it left and you want it to go right, you have to stop 5 feet of sword and start it again, and that costs you a beat, and that beat is where everything happens in a fight with these things.

Hands apart, one of them up on the blade — now you've got a lever with two ends. Push with the left, pull with the right and the sword turns over about a point between your hands instead of about your grip. It's like a poler's pole. It doesn't have to be stopped and restarted. It rolls over.

I've counted it in the yard against a post. Hands together, high cut to the left, then a high cut to the right: 3 beats. Hands apart, same two cuts: 2 beats, and the second one arrives with about as much behind it.

That's the whole thing. Not speed. TURNOVER. Cray's measuring the first blow. The first blow's never mattered. It's the second one that gets a man, because the first one told him something and he moved, and if you're there before he's finished moving you've got him.

WHAT THAT MEANS IN A FIGHT.

Against Cray's hanging guard — and I'll say now the hanging guard is right, I use it, everyone should use it, it's the best thing in his book — the difference shows up the moment somebody steps inside.

Cray teaches: step back once, keep the guard, let him come to a stop, then drop. And that's good and it works and it's how I was beaten by his second-best pupil twice before I worked it out.

But if he's stepped back and I've come on and I'm inside his arc, the man with the hands together has one answer, which is the pommel and the crossguard, and it's a good answer. The man with the hands apart has the whole middle of the sword available as a short weapon straight away, because his left hand is already on the blade and the thing is already half a staff. I don't have to change anything. I'm already holding it the way you'd hold it if you were close.

That's why we win the second minute. First minute belongs to reach and Cray's people have the reach. Second minute, when everyone's inside everyone and tired, belongs to whoever's holding something they can still use.

ON THE MUD, WHICH NOBODY IN CHORROL HAS EVER STOOD IN.

Also — and I'd have led with this if I could write proper — the long reach isn't worth what he thinks it's worth here.

Reach costs you footwork. To use 5 feet of sword you've got to be able to step in and step out, and stepping out is the half of it people forget. In Blackrose in the wet season you can't step out. You can lean out. Your back foot is where your back foot is and it's 6 inches into something and it's staying there.

So the fen lads fight standing more or less still and turning, and a method built on turning over beats a method built on stepping back, on ground where nobody steps back.

The Chorrol schools are right about everything except where they are.

LAST.

Master Cray says when I'm 40 my wrists will have gone. He's 61 and he says it like a curse.

My mother's brother held a sword this way for 30 years in Dunstad and he died of a fever with both wrists working. I don't think the wrists are the reason. I think the reason is he saw his best pupils lose to fen lads in a yard, and he's 61, and there's nothing in a book that can fix that, and I'd not have printed mine if he'd just taken the bout.

Offer's still open, Master. No edges. First to 5 touches. I'll come to your yard and I'll not say a word after.

books.title: The Reaper and the Scythe: On the Long Curved Blades, and on Lending Them to the Living
books.author: Teeus-Ahai, compiling, and this time against the advice of everyone at Soulrest
books.unreliability: A compiler's book. He has assembled every account he could find of the drowned reapers being carried by living people and has not decided what he thinks, and says so, and then arranges the accounts in an order that decides it for the reader. The dating of the Soulrest procession is his own guess presented as a record.

contradicts.on: whether the reaping blades were ever weapons before the Duskfall

books.text:
I have been told by three keepers and by my own household not to write this, and the reason given each time was the same: that the reaping blades are not a subject, they are a duty, and a duty does not have a history.

I say a duty that nobody may write about becomes a duty nobody remembers the shape of. I have made this argument before, about the chronicle, and was disregarded, and the chronicle exists.

WHAT THESE THINGS ARE.

A long curved blade on a long shaft, the edge on the inside of the curve, swung in a full revolution so that the wielder turns with it and comes back round to where they began.

Nobody who has seen one used forgets it. The motion is not like any other weapon in this province. Every other long weapon goes out and comes back. This one goes round, and the person goes round with it, and the whole of it — blade, shaft, arms, hips, feet — is a single turning thing that arrives from a direction the eye did not have time to choose.

There are two patterns and the whole of my difficulty is in the difference between them.

THE FIRST PATTERN. THE REAPER OF THE DROWNED.

Carried in procession at Soulrest, at Lilmoth, at the drowned shrines on the Topal shore, and at Helstrom on the one night. The shaft is grown, not cut. The blade is set to sweep level at the height of a standing person's waist.

Every account I have of these agrees that they are ceremonial. Not one account I have of these describes a ceremony in which nothing was cut.

I set that sentence down and I let it sit.

THE SECOND PATTERN. THE MIRE SCYTHE.

A harvest scythe, re-hafted. The tang turned, the blade set to tip downward instead of running level, the shaft shortened and given a second grip.

These are recent. I have found none that anybody claims is older than the Knahaten years and I have found 30 that families date to that period exactly, which is what happens when a country has to arm itself in a hurry and has a great many scythes.

The difference in the hang of the blade is not decoration. A level blade sweeps. A tipped blade ploughs — it goes into the ground if you let it, and the people who use them say this is the point, because a blade that will bite the earth will certainly bite a leg, and because a stroke that ends in the ground has somewhere to stop.

The reapers have nowhere to stop. That is said of them by everyone who carries one.

THE ACCOUNTS.

I set these out in the order I received them and not in the order they happened, and a reader who wants the other order may make it.

*The Soulrest procession, in the year of the second census.* A keeper's leave-book records that the reapers were carried out and carried back and that two were not carried back and that no explanation was entered. The same book records the purchase of 3 new shafts the following season. Nothing else. I have asked at Soulrest and been told the book is wrong, and when I asked in what way, I was told: in the way that books are.

*The lane at Stormhold.* Told to me at Thorn by an auxiliary who was not there, from a serjeant who was. A raiding party came up the water stair into a lane 4 paces wide. A single person with a reaper held the lane for as long as it took the boats to be got off, and did it by turning, and by never once stopping the turn, so that anybody entering the lane entered a wheel. The serjeant's phrase, given to me at third hand and therefore not to be trusted: *it was like arguing with a mill.*

*The Duskfall claim.* Three separate households at Lilmoth hold that the reaping blades are older than the Duskfall and were weapons first and became duties afterwards. Two of the three cannot say where they learned it. The third showed me a blade she said was proof, and it was very old and it was very plainly a farm tool that had been re-hafted at some point by somebody competent, and when I said so she said that was the point and I did not follow, and she would not say it a second way.

*Against all of the above.* The keeper at Helstrom who refused to speak to me for this book made one remark as I was leaving, and I record it because it is the only argument on the other side that has any weight in it: she said that a thing used once in a hundred years to cut something is not a weapon, it is a knife in a kitchen, and the Empire has one word for both and we should not borrow their word.

WHAT I THINK, WHICH IS LESS THAN I WOULD LIKE.

I think the two-handed reaping blades were made for a duty and are a serious weapon, and I do not think those two facts are in tension, and I think the discomfort at Soulrest is about the second fact being said out loud rather than about it being untrue.

I think the mire scythes are what happens when people who have watched a duty performed all their lives need something in their hands in a bad year, and copy the only long blade they have ever seen used well, and improve it by accident by making it stop.

And I think — though this is a guess and I mark it a guess — that a weapon which cannot be recalled once begun was never going to be popular with people who have to live among each other afterwards, and that the procession is where such a thing survives.

I will be told I have written a book about a duty. I have. I would rather be told off for it than have my grandchildren find one of these in a store-room and wonder what it was for.
